sections.h2: Warren County offices that handle property tax
sections.html:
Two elected offices split the work. The Warren County Auditor values property and administers credits. The Warren County Treasurer sends the bills and takes payment. The auditor's office is at 406 Justice Drive in Lebanon, and its real estate department answers at 513-695-1235.

The auditor keeps records on about 91,400 parcels, covering ownership, legal description, property address, building description, appraised value and the transfer history that feeds the tax list. The treasurer posts rate sheets for every year from 2004 through 2025, so you can look up how your parcel's levies have moved.

Complaints about value go to the Board of Revision, a panel of three that seats the auditor, the treasurer and the commissioners' president.

sections.h2: How the county values a house
sections.html:
Each parcel is appraised at estimated fair market value and taxed at 35 percent of it, which is Ohio's common level of assessment. A general reappraisal includes a site visit to every parcel at least once every six years. A triennial update adjusts values in the third year between those cycles, usually by percentage changes drawn from local sales.

New construction and changes in use are valued every year. The tax lien date is January 1, so ownership and use on that day fix the bill payable the following year.

Most increases follow the state-required reappraisal, and without new construction or new levies, bills tend to stay near the same level between updates. A school levy passed by voters in a district raises bills for the parcels inside it, which is why two similar homes in different school districts can pay different amounts.

sections.h2: Due dates and how to pay
sections.html:
Ohio real estate tax is billed in two halves, with the first half due in February and the second half in the summer. The treasurer announces exact dates each year. In years when the state delays the second-half bills, wait for the bill instead of sending an estimate.

You can pay through the myWarrenCountyOhio portal, by calling 513-496-2931, or in person weekdays between 7:30 am and 4:30 pm. The treasurer's page posts these forms:

  • Application for Remission of Late Payment Penalties.
  • Military Extension Application.
  • Notice of Possible Tax Adjustment.

Late charges come from Revised Code 323.121. An unpaid half draws a ten percent penalty, cut in half when the whole amount arrives within ten days of the deadline. Delinquent balances also collect interest at the rate set under section 5703.47.

sections.h2: Appealing a Warren County property value
sections.html:
If you believe the auditor's value is too high, form DTE 1 is the tool. The auditor accepts it from January 1 through March 31 of the next tax year, and a notary must witness the signature of the owner or the owner's attorney.

The board decides market value for land and buildings together, never the tax dollars or rates. The owner carries the burden of proof, so a weak case can leave the value alone or even push it up. The board sends notice at least ten days before the recorded hearing and later mails or emails a decision letter to each party.

  • Good evidence includes a recent sale for less than the county's value, a recent fee appraisal, and proof of damage or defects that hurt the home's worth.
  • The board may also request purchase or lease agreements, closing statements, construction cost records, rent rolls and income and expense statements.
  • Get supporting papers to the board before the hearing date.

sections.h2: Homestead, owner-occupied credit and other breaks
sections.html:
The auditor runs several programs, and each ties to your principal residence on January 1. A person can claim a homestead or owner-occupied reduction on only one Ohio home.

Homeowner credits and the value appeal
ProgramWho qualifiesForm and filing window
Homestead exemption65 or older; permanently and totally disabled; or surviving spouse, 59 or olderForm DTE 105A, in the auditor's hands by December 31
Owner-occupied creditOwner who lives in the home on January 1Form DTE 105C, filed by December 31 of the year claimed
Value complaintOwner who disputes market valueForm DTE 1, filed between January 1 and March 31

The homestead income cap for the 2026 tax year was $41,000 of 2025 Ohio adjusted gross income. Owners who miss the cutoff can reapply the next year, when the state may raise it. A disability claim needs Certificate of Disability form DTE 105E or another accepted certification.

Two other reductions are worth a look. Damaged or destroyed buildings can earn a value deduction on form DTE 26, filed by December 31 for damage in the first nine months of a year or by January 31 for damage in the last three. The share granted depends on the quarter: 100 percent for January to March, 75 for April to June, 50 for July to September and 25 for October to December. Farmland in the CAUV program is valued on expected farm income. It is open to farms over 10 acres in commercial use for three years and to smaller ones grossing at least $2,500 a year, with a $25 first-time filing fee and a payback of up to three years of savings if the use changes.

sections.h2: What changes on the tax side at a sale
sections.html:
The auditor transfers the deed on the tax list before the recorder sees it. Three charges apply: a conveyance fee, a county transfer tax and a per-parcel transfer fee. All are due before the deed goes on to the recorder.

The state's statement of value, set out in section 319.202, asks whether the home's taxes are reduced under the homestead or owner-occupied credit statute, and whether the land carried CAUV value. A yes means a sworn paper estimating the reduction or the recoupment, signed by buyer and seller. The statement also reminds the buyer to tell the auditor if the home later stops qualifying for the reduction.

One more Ohio rule applies to landlords. When the house is residential rental property, the auditor's endorsement on the deed tells the new owner to file rental registration information.

Before listing, ask the treasurer for a written payoff covering penalties and interest. The title company will want it for the closing statement. The Application for Remission of Late Payment Penalties is the way to ask for relief on penalties.

The county also runs forfeited land sales for parcels with long unpaid balances. Ask either office how a delinquent parcel moves toward that kind of sale, and settle the balance early.

Here is a simple order of work for a seller with taxes owed:

  • Get the payoff figure from the treasurer.
  • Decide whether to pay it now or have the title company pay it from your proceeds at closing.
  • File the penalty remission application if a late charge looks unfair.

A cash buyer can close quickly, but the payoff still has to be settled, so start with the treasurer.

faqs.q: Who sends the property tax bill in Warren County, Ohio?
faqs.a: The Warren County Treasurer does. The auditor sets the value, and the treasurer bills, collects and posts rate sheets. You can pay through myWarrenCountyOhio or by phone at 513-496-2931.

faqs.q: What percent of market value does Warren County tax?
faqs.a: Thirty-five percent of appraised value is the taxable value. The auditor reappraises every parcel at least once in six years and updates values in the third year between.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to challenge a Warren County valuation?
faqs.a: March 31 closes the window. A DTE 1 complaint can go to the auditor starting January 1 of the following tax year, and the signature has to be notarized.

faqs.q: What income limit applies to the Warren County homestead exemption?
faqs.a: For the 2026 tax year the limit was $41,000 of 2025 Ohio adjusted gross income. You must be 65, permanently disabled, or a surviving spouse who is at least 59, and the application must reach the auditor by December 31.

faqs.q: Can I get Warren County late-payment penalties removed?
faqs.a: You can apply. The treasurer posts an Application for Remission of Late Payment Penalties and a Military Extension Application. Under Ohio law, paying the full amount within ten days of the due date also cuts the penalty in half.
